tier_reason: Independent measurement: OpenJDK maintainer Alan Bateman's JMH run (SelectOne.testSelectOne, avgt ns/op, Cnt 20) in reviewed and integrated openjdk/jdk PR 3816 shows the wepoll-based Selector flat at 1428.914-1445.201 ns/op versus the select()-based Selector rising from 1587.429 to 932032.385 ns/op for 1 to 10000 channels. The benchmark code is public (test/micro/org/openjdk/bench/java/nio/channels/SelectOne.java) but CPU model, JDK build and compiler flags are not stated, so not A.

corrections.caveats: The only numbers are third-party and indirect. They come from an OpenJDK maintainer's JMH run of the JDK Selector built on wepoll (PR 3816, Windows Server 2019), so the roughly 1.4 us floor includes JVM/JNI and Selector overhead, and the gain at 1 channel is only about 1.1x. The baseline is the JDK's own select() Selector (WindowsSelectorImpl), not WSAPoll, IOCP, or raw select() in C; that selector caps each select() call at MAX_SELECTABLE_FDS = 1024 and adds one helper thread per further 1023 channels, so the 10000-channel row (about 645x) also includes helper-thread coordination, while the 100 and 1000 rows are a single linear select(). One ready socket only; the PR notes an exception (select after wakeup) where the old Selector skips selection and gives no number. CPU model and JDK build flags are not stated, and the PR rows show Cnt 20 while the current benchmark file in openjdk/jdk (test/micro/org/openjdk/bench/java/nio/channels/SelectOne.java) uses @Fork(3) with 5 warmup and 5 measurement iterations, so rerunning would use different settings. wepoll's own README makes only qualitative claims ('fast and scalable', 'can poll 100000s of sockets efficiently') with no numbers. No commits since 2020-11-30 on master (default branch dist last updated 2020-06-29, version 1.5.8); the maintenance status follows the over-3-years rule, but the library is stable and still vendored: openjdk/jdk master carries src/java.base/windows/native/libnio/ch/wepoll.c and its Windows DefaultSelectorProvider is WEPollSelectorProvider.

notes: Record accurate: all ten ns/op figures match the PR page, ratios correctly marked derived, BSD-2-Clause confirmed from LICENSE, 1.1k stars, last master commit 2020-11-30, not archived. Shortcomings to record: indirect measurement through the JDK NIO Selector, baseline is the JDK's select()-based Selector with helper threads beyond 1023 channels (not raw select/WSAPoll/IOCP), CPU and build flags unstated, one ready socket only, no first-party numbers, abandoned since 2020 but still vendored in OpenJDK.

tier_reason: Only numbers are a 4-star third-party Ruby binding's own README table (tlewin/ruby-uriparser, benchmark/benchmark.rb) timing UriParser.parse against Ruby's URI.parse; the code is public but the C compiler and flags are unstated (extconf.rb uses mkmf defaults) and the CPU is given only as a 2.7 GHz Dual-Core Intel Core i5, and the wrapper author is measuring his own gem, so it is not an independent suite and stays C.

corrections.caveats: Weak evidence for the uriparser C library itself. The only numbers found are from a third-party Ruby binding (tlewin/ruby-uriparser, MIT, 4 stars, last commit 2021-03-25) timing a C parse against the pure-Ruby stdlib, so the gap is mostly compiled C versus interpreted Ruby and says nothing about uriparser against any C or C++ URI parser (Ada, Boost.URL, curl, Poco, QUrl). The two sides do unequal work: the wrapper's UriParser.parse (ext/uriparser_ext/uriparser.c) calls uriParseUriA and wraps the result, but creates the Ruby strings for scheme, userinfo, host, port, path, query and fragment lazily on first access, and the benchmark never reads them, while URI.parse builds a full URI::HTTPS object with all component strings. The 7.5x headline does not match the README's own table (4.5x-5.5x on the measured pass; 7.3x only on the rehearsal pass for complex URLs). The simple-URL row times Kernel#URI(...) for the Ruby baseline vs UriParser.parse. README says 100,000 calls while benchmark/benchmark.rb defaults to 10,000 unless an argument is passed. The C extension is built by mkmf with Ruby's default flags (extconf.rb sets none) against a system uriparser of unstated version. Single run, one machine. uriparser's own README says only 'fast' with no numbers; its ChangeLog, GOALS.txt and repo tree hold no benchmark. ada-url/ada's benchmarks/bench.cpp includes a BasicBench_uriparser_just_parse competitor (behind the ADA_COMPETITION CMake option, OFF by default) that could measure uriparser against curl, but no published uriparser numbers from it were found (ada's README chart lists only ada, servo url and curl). Licensing: the library is BSD-3-Clause, the test suite LGPL-2.1-or-later and the fuzzing code Apache-2.0 (GitHub shows 'Apache-2.0 and 2 other licenses'); all OSI-approved. A previous pass (w3-mine-h) filed uriparser as no evidence; this record exists only because of the wrapper's table.

notes: Numbers verified on the ruby-uriparser README (measured pass complex 1.138771 vs 0.207083 s total, simple 0.710042 vs 0.157204 s; rehearsal complex 1.146867 vs 0.156927 s); metadata confirmed (416 stars, last commit 2026-07-27, BSD-3-Clause core). Not a duplicate: the binding is only the evidence source, uriparser itself is not otherwise listed. Shortcomings to record: evidence comes only from a 4-star third-party Ruby binding versus pure-Ruby URI.parse (C versus interpreter, no C/C++ baseline), the wrapper defers component string creation so it does less work per call than URI.parse, headline 7.5x overstates the measured 4.5-5.5x, flags and uriparser version unstated, single run.
